summary:
West Kalimantan records no separate LGBTI legislation and no documented provincial enforcement, so the national framework of Indonesia governs what a trans visitor faces in the province.

Indonesia's penal code, signed in December 2022 and in force from 2 January 2026, penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Provincial morality laws elsewhere in the country and Aceh's caning punishments, imposed under provincial religious law, form part of the enforcement texture a visitor may encounter on inter-provincial travel. Aceh's penalties apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising. Vigilante mobs attacked transgender women across Indonesia in a wave of 14-16 July 2026, among them more than 15 trans women who were doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor, with footage of the attack shared online. A presidential decree of October 2025 lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among non-military threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction, placing LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy, and reporting of August 2026 ties the surge in attacks directly to that decree and to officials' public condemnations.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents and screening carry exposure. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors with no third-gender or X option, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution does not address either.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; his mother in Lima was told during a WhatsApp call that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and she alleges police beat him; Indonesian police deny that violence was used.
tangentialFactors:
Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside the national morality provisions. Neither borders West Kalimantan, but their existence means a visitor moving between provinces can cross from a regime of national provisions alone into one carrying provincial penalties, and the Aceh caning of February 2025 shows those penalties reaching people for conduct that is not separately criminalised under the national code.

A researcher cited in reporting of August 2026 documents markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016, which the reporting links to the rise in vigilante attacks rather than to any change in statute. Public statements by officials are named as a driver alongside the October 2025 presidential decree.

West Kalimantan's position as a province on Borneo, sharing a land border with Malaysia, is not addressed in the source inventory, so cross-border movement effects on document screening are unresolved rather than documented.
localsOnly:
Transgender Indonesians who do not hide their identity often struggle to keep legitimate employment, and some are pushed into sex work as a result. This is a resident-facing economic condition rather than a rule applied at the border.

On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected a conservative petition 5-4 that had sought to criminalise homosexuality and extramarital sex, declining to add them to the Penal Code. The judgment removed a route to expanded criminalisation but did not create a protection, and no national non-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity.

A global survey reports that discrimination and harassment are not uncommon among LGBTI Indonesians, while direct violence is reported as rare. The survey's sample, methodology and reference date are not stated in the sources.

Legal gender change follows a single route nationwide: sex reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, with no third-gender or X marker available on identity documents.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source set contains no West Kalimantan-specific reporting on enforcement, raids, arrests or local bylaws. Whether the province has adopted its own morality provisions, and whether any have been applied, is unresolved rather than affirmatively documented as absent.

The encyclopedia entry for West Kalimantan yielded no usable finding for this profile, so the province-level layer rests on a single source.

The status of the 2025 bill on online content presenting LGBT behaviour, including whether it has been enacted, is not resolved in the sources. The same applies to whether any prosecution has been brought under the penal code provisions that took effect on 2 January 2026, in this province or elsewhere.

The circumstances of Rodrigo Ventocilla's death in custody rest on conflicting accounts, his mother's allegation of beating against the police denial, and the sources do not record any judicial outcome. The figure of up to US$100,000 is reported as an allegation, not a documented official demand.

The reported 14-16 July 2026 attacks are located in Bogor and elsewhere in the country; no source in the inventory places anti-trans mob violence in West Kalimantan specifically.
